sections.h2: Which Lawrenceburg offices touch an Anderson County tax bill?
sections.html:
The Sheriff, at 208 S Main St, collects the money and answers questions at (502) 839-4021 Monday to Friday during office hours of 7 to 5. The Property Valuation Administrator, at (502) 839-4061, sets the assessed value the bill rests on. Alton, McBrayer and the other crossroads places in this 202-square-mile county use the same two offices as Lawrenceburg, the only city.

Bills leave the Sheriff's Office in the final days of September and money is accepted starting October 1. Lenders are no longer mailed copies, so a homeowner with an escrow account should phone the servicer in October to learn whether the bill arrived.

The county takes its name from Richard Clough Anderson Jr., a legislator and later U.S. minister to Colombia. A General Assembly act of January 28, 1854 changed the line between Anderson and Franklin counties, so owners near that edge can ask the PVA to confirm which county bills the parcel.

sections.h2: How fast does an unpaid Anderson County bill grow?
sections.html:
The Sheriff's tax page lays out the schedule that KRS 134.015 sets for all counties. Payment can be made with cash, a check or a money order. Installments are refused, and a postmark earns nothing because the office needs the funds in hand by the date.

Anderson County Sheriff tax bill stages with the effect on the amount owed
StageDatesEffect on the amount
EarlyOctober 1 to November 12 percent discount
PlainNovember 2 to December 31The printed amount
First penaltyJanuary 1 to 31Five percent on top
Second penaltyFebruary 1 until the office shuts on April 15Ten percent, plus ten percent more as the Sheriff's fee

Take an invented $2,000 bill. It costs $1,960 in the discount month, $2,000 in November and December, and $2,100 in January. From February the state's own sample shows the add-on being figured on the tax plus penalty, so the bill becomes $2,000 plus $200 plus $220, or $2,420. From best month to worst the gap is $460.

After that last day the bill is no longer the Sheriff's problem. At the County Clerk it turns into a certificate of delinquency. The Sheriff's page lists the extras: 20 percent for the County Attorney, 10 percent for the Clerk, and 1 percent interest each month. Summer can bring a sale to an outside buyer.

sections.h2: What does a $1,000 bill turn into at the clerk's counter?
sections.html:
In the state revenue agency's worked case, $1,000 owed grows to $1,254 when the Sheriff hands it off, after a penalty, the add-on and an assumed 4 percent commission. The case then totals $1,387.79 if paid within five business days and $1,611.30 once the county attorney's first letter is out. Because commission rates differ, an Anderson County owner should request a real payoff from the clerk.

The first letter goes out within a month of the handoff. KRS 134.128 puts the tax sale between 90 and 135 days after the transfer, with advertising in print and online.

Before April 15 the Sheriff handles everything. Afterward the clerk's website offers a delinquent-tax lookup called DTax. Its page says the data is informational and the clerk alone decides the actual dollar amount for each bill at the time of any sale. Owners with an old balance should therefore get a written payoff from the office instead of relying on a screen.

sections.h2: Is it worth contesting a valuation in Anderson County?
sections.html:
The sequence cannot be shuffled. Assessments reflect January 1. Anyone may inspect the roll for 13 days starting the first Monday of May, and a meeting with the PVA or a deputy has to happen before an appeal. The County Clerk takes the appeal until the day after inspection ends.

The local appeals board convenes 25 to 35 days after inspection closes and sits for as many as five. It expects paper: land and building descriptions, insurance policies, what construction cost, and sales listings. A bare filing loses. Staying home from the hearing ends the appeal, and a final value over your claim means an extra bill.

sections.h2: Does an Anderson County senior pay less?
sections.html:
A homeowner at least 65 years old, or classified as totally disabled, can apply to the PVA. The state exemption is worth $49,100 of assessed value for 2025 and 2026 and is reset every other year. On a house assessed at $225,100 it would leave $176,000 to tax.

A birth certificate, license or passport proves age. A disability claim is renewed each year, except for veterans with a service-connected disability and owners found permanently and totally disabled by Social Security or Kentucky Retirement Systems.

sections.h2: What has population growth done to Anderson County housing?
sections.html:
Anderson County had 4,520 residents in 1830, fell from 7,404 in 1860 to 5,449 in 1870, then rose to 14,571 in 1990 and 23,852 in 2020. An estimate for mid-2025 reads 25,225. Wikipedia calls it the ninth fastest-growing and 48th most populated of Kentucky's counties. The median age in 2020 was 42.0, and 56.8 percent of residents lived in urban areas.

Houses follow people: 10,652 housing units stood in the county in July 2025, and 147 building permits were issued for 2025. Owners can compare their assessments with recent neighborhood sales before the roll opens.

About 90.4 percent of residents lived at the same address a year earlier, and 94.5 percent of households have a computer, so most owners can look up a parcel online or call the PVA without much trouble.

  • Median owner-occupied home value in the 2020 to 2024 survey: $225,100.
  • Households that own: 77.6 percent of 9,653.
  • Midpoint household income: $74,488; midpoint gross rent: $927.
  • Monthly owner costs: $1,391 with a mortgage and $411 without.

Someone who bought last year can list the deed price as next January's value if the home is unchanged.

In 2023 the county held 352 employer establishments with 4,175 jobs and $189.3 million in payroll. Shops sold $338.8 million in 2022. Some 60.2 percent of residents over 16 work or look for work, and the average trip to work takes 30.4 minutes.

Among adults, 90.5 percent have a high school diploma and 26.2 percent a bachelor's degree or higher. Broadband reaches 88.7 percent of households, 1,350 residents are veterans, and 22.0 percent are children.

The 2020 count found 9,369 households and 10,044 housing units, of which 6.7 percent stood vacant. Rental vacancy was 3.8 percent against 1.3 percent for owned homes, and 22.4 percent of households were headed by a woman with no partner present..

sections.h2: How do I clear taxes before I sell in Lawrenceburg or elsewhere in the county?
sections.html:
• Call the Sheriff for the live balance, earlier years included, or the Clerk after April 15.
  • Let the closing agent pay arrears from your share and file the release.
  • Give the deed the buyer's mailing address for next year's bill (KRS 382.135).
  • If you hold a homestead exemption, tell the PVA about the sale.

If you are behind on taxes and want to skip repairs, request a written cash offer. Taxes and clerk charges are taken from the price at closing.

faqs.q: Until what date does the discount last?
faqs.a: Through November 1. KRS 134.015 gives 2 percent off to a taxpayer paying in full by then. Between November 2 and year end the printed amount applies.

faqs.q: What happens if I wait until February?
faqs.a: The Sheriff's schedule adds a 10 percent penalty and a further 10 percent Sheriff's fee to the printed amount, from February 1 until April 15.

faqs.q: Can I pay in two halves?
faqs.a: No. Partial payments are not taken, and a check that arrives after the cutoff counts as late whatever its postmark.

faqs.q: What do I do first if the value looks too high?
faqs.a: Ask the PVA's office for a conference. The County Clerk cannot accept an appeal without one, and the filing deadline falls on the workday after inspection ends.

faqs.q: What is the homestead exemption worth?
faqs.a: It is worth $49,100 of assessed value for 2025 and 2026. Owners who are 65 or older or totally disabled apply at the PVA.
